chapters.title: Chapter 0: Purpose and Learning Outcomes
chapters.content:
Purpose

A retail transaction is not complete when the customer leaves the store.

The retailer must:

  • Successfully authorize payment
  • Capture funds
  • Settle with financial institutions
  • Reconcile transactions
  • Detect fraud
  • Protect sensitive customer data

Meet regulatory and compliance requirements

A store may survive inventory issues for days.

A widespread payment outage can immediately stop revenue generation.

This module provides the domain knowledge needed to understand payment systems, payment failures, compliance requirements, risk management, fraud detection, and operational response.

Learning Outcomes

By the end of this module, learners should be able to:

  • ✅ Explain end-to-end retail payment processing
  • ✅ Distinguish authorization, capture, settlement, and reconciliation
  • ✅ Understand common payment failure scenarios
  • ✅ Explain PCI compliance boundaries
  • ✅ Identify fraud indicators
  • ✅ Classify payment incidents by severity
  • ✅ Create payment response playbooks
  • ✅ Design AI agents for payment intelligence and incident triage

How Developers Should Use This Module

  • Treat payment as a regulated state machine, not a single API outcome.
  • Model every financial transition with traceability and replay-safe behavior.
  • Design for customer safety first during uncertain outcomes (timeouts, retries, duplicate risk).

Core Engineering Questions

  • What is the current payment state and who owns the next legal transition?
  • How is idempotency enforced across auth, capture, refund, and reversal calls?
  • Which evidence is needed to prove compliance and resolve disputes?

checkpoint.answer: Funds must be captured, settled, and reconciled, not just authorized.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Payment Ecosystem Fundamentals
chapters.content:
Why Payments Matter

Every retail transaction ultimately becomes a financial transaction.

Example:

  1. Customer Buys Product
  2. Card Authorization
  3. Approved Sale
  4. Settlement
  5. Money Arrives To Retailer

A successful sale only becomes revenue after funds are successfully settled.

  • Retail Payment Participants

Customer

Initiates payment.

Examples:

  • Cash
  • Credit Card
  • Debit Card
  • Gift Card
  • Mobile Wallet
  • Merchant

Retailer accepting payment.

Examples:

  • HEB
  • Target
  • Costco
  • Walmart
  • Payment Gateway

Routes payment requests.

Responsibilities:

  • Encryption
  • Routing
  • Security
  • Response Handling
  • Card Network

Issues payment routing standards.

Examples:

  • Visa
  • Mastercard
  • American Express
  • Discover
  • Issuer Bank

Customer's bank.

Responsibilities:

  • Verify Account
  • Verify Funds
  • Approve Or Decline
  • Acquirer Bank

Retailer's bank.

Receives funds after settlement.

Payment Processing Overview

  1. Customer
  2. POS
  3. Payment Gateway
  4. Card Network
  5. Issuer Bank
  6. Approval/Decline
  7. POS

Participant Contracts

ParticipantRoleCritical Output
POS/CommerceInitiates payment intentCanonical request payload
GatewayRoutes and normalizes transactionsGateway reference + response code
NetworkScheme transport/rulesAuthorization routing decision
IssuerFunds/risk decisionApprove/Decline result
AcquirerMerchant settlement pathCapture/settlement outcome

Developer Invariants

  • Never lose linkage between internal transaction ID and external payment references.
  • Response code taxonomy must be mapped to deterministic retry/fail policies.
  • Terminal and backend timestamps need synchronized audit order.

checkpoint.answer: Because incident ownership and escalation depend on where failure occurs in the payment chain.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Authorization
chapters.content:
What is Authorization?

Authorization asks:

Is This Payment Allowed?

The issuer validates:

  • Card Validity
  • Available Funds
  • Fraud Checks
  • Account Status
  • Authorization Flow
  1. Customer Taps Card
  2. POS Sends Request
  3. Gateway Processes
  4. Issuer Bank Evaluates
  5. Response Returned
  • Possible Responses
  • Approved
  • Customer May Continue

Declined

Examples:

  • Insufficient Funds
  • Expired Card
  • Blocked Card
  • Fraud Suspicion
  • Timeout

Issuer does not respond in time.

Risk:

  • Customer Retries
  • Possible Duplicate Charges
  • Key Authorization Metrics
  • Authorization Success Rate
  • Average Response Time
  • Decline Rate
  • Timeout Rate

Authorization Request Contract

  • merchantOrderId, amount, currency, tender type
  • idempotencyKey, correlationId, channel/store/terminal metadata
  • risk context (if available): device/customer/session signals

Outcome Handling

OutcomeMeaningRequired System Action
ApprovedFunds reserved/authorizedMove to capture-eligible state
DeclinedIssuer deniedOffer alternate tender, persist code
TimeoutUnknown final stateReconcile before retrying new auth

checkpoint.answer: No, authorization only reserves/permits payment; capture and settlement must still occur.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Capture
chapters.content:
What is Capture?

Authorization reserves funds.

Capture requests funds transfer.

Important distinction:

  • Authorization ≠ Payment Received
  • Example

Customer spends:

$100

Authorization:

Funds Reserved

Capture:

Funds Requested

Settlement:

  • Funds Delivered
  • Capture Models
  • Immediate Capture

Common in retail.

  1. Sale
  2. Capture

Delayed Capture

Common in:

  • Hotels
  • Travel
  • E-Commerce

Products may ship later.

Capture Semantics

  • Capture converts authorization hold into settlement-eligible funds movement.
  • Capture may be full or partial depending on business flow.
  • Capture must reference original authorization deterministically.

Failure Controls

  • Prevent duplicate capture with capture idempotency keys.
  • Track uncaptured authorization aging and auto-escalate before expiry.
  • Ensure partial-capture accounting remains consistent with order totals.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the key distinction of capture?
checkpoint.answer: Capture initiates fund transfer after authorization.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Settlement
chapters.content:
What is Settlement?

Settlement moves money between institutions.

  1. Customer Bank
  2. Card Network
  3. Acquirer
  4. Retailer Account

Settlement Timeline

Example:

  • Day 1
  • Sale Occurs
  • Day 2
  • Settlement Batch Sent
  • Day 3
  • Funds Received
  • Settlement Risks

Missing Settlement

Authorization approved.

Settlement fails.

Impact:

Customer Charged

  • Retailer Unpaid

Duplicate Settlement

Transaction submitted twice.

Impact:

  • Customer Complaints
  • Chargebacks
  • Refund Work

Settlement Pipeline

  1. Collect captured transactions
  2. Create settlement batch
  3. Submit to acquirer/network
  4. Receive settlement confirmations/exceptions
  5. Post financial entries and variance signals

Operational Risks

  • Missing batch submission windows
  • Batch-level rejects due to malformed records
  • Mismatch between captured amount and settled amount

checkpoint.prompt: Why can sales and cash disagree temporarily?
checkpoint.answer: Because settlement and bank posting can lag checkout completion.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Payment Reconciliation
chapters.content:
Why Reconciliation Exists

Retail systems and payment systems do not always agree.

Reconciliation verifies consistency.

Example

POS Reports:

  • 100 Transactions
  • $10,000 Sales

Gateway Reports:

  • 98 Transactions
  • $9,800

Difference:

$200 Variance

Investigation required.

  • Reconciliation Sources
  • POS
  • Payment Gateway
  • Settlement Files

Bank Reports

  • ERP

Reconciliation Process

  1. Collect Data
  2. Compare Records
  3. Find Variance
  4. Root Cause Analysis
  5. Adjust Or Correct
  • Common Variances
  • Duplicate Transaction
  • Missing Capture
  • Settlement Failure
  • Offline Upload Delay
  • Batch Failure

Three-Way Reconciliation

SourceCompared AgainstGoal
POS/Order SystemGateway transactionsNo missing/duplicate payment attempts
GatewayAcquirer settlement reports
Settlement recordsFinance postings

Variance Handling

  • Classify mismatch type: missing, duplicate, amount mismatch, status mismatch.
  • Assign owner and SLA by variance criticality.
  • Preserve full evidence timeline for audit and dispute workflows.

checkpoint.answer: Collect and align records from all source systems before root-cause analysis.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Payment Failure Taxonomy
chapters.content:
Payment-related incidents are among the highest-priority retail events.

Category 1: Authorization Failures

Symptoms:

  • High Decline Rate
  • Payment Unavailable

Root Causes:

  • Issuer Outage
  • Gateway Issue
  • Network Connectivity

Category 2: Transaction Timeouts

Symptoms:

  • Long Wait Times
  • Repeated Tries

Impact:

  • Abandoned Sales
  • Duplicate Payments

Category 3: Duplicate Charges

Symptoms:

Multiple Authorizations

Business Impact:

  • Customer Complaints
  • Chargebacks
  • Brand Damage

Category 4: Settlement Failure

Symptoms:

  • Completed Sales
  • Missing Deposits

Impact:

  • Revenue Recognition Problems
  • Manual Investigation Required

Category 5: Gift Card Failures

Symptoms:

  • Incorrect Balance
  • Rejected Transactions

Impact:

  • Customer Escalations
  • Store Delays

Failure Classification Dimensions

  • Stage: auth, capture, settlement, refund, reversal
  • Type: timeout, decline, duplicate, mismatch, integration defect
  • Blast radius: single transaction, store cluster, cross-channel

First Response Pattern

  • Identify failure stage and dominant error code group.
  • Quantify impacted payment attempts and revenue-at-risk.
  • Apply safest containment before broad retries.

checkpoint.answer: Authorization failures, timeouts, and duplicate charge incidents.

chapters.title: Chapter 7: PCI Compliance Fundamentals
chapters.content:
What is PCI?

PCI DSS:

Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard

Industry framework for protecting cardholder data.

Why PCI Matters

Failure can result in:

  • Financial Penalties
  • Legal Risk
  • Reputation Damage
  • Security Breaches
  • Sensitive Information

Examples:

  • Card Number (PAN)
  • CVV
  • Track Data
  • PIN Data

Must be protected.

PCI Boundary

Systems within PCI scope:

  • POS
  • PIN Pads
  • Payment Applications
  • Payment Networks
  • PCI Objectives
  • Protect Cardholder Data
  • Encrypt Sensitive Information
  • Limit Access
  • Maintain Audit Logs
  • Monitor Security Events

PCI Scope Modeling

  • Identify every system that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data.
  • Segment card-data environment from general application workloads.
  • Use tokenization to reduce direct PAN exposure where possible.

Developer Controls

  • Never log PAN/CVV or sensitive auth data.
  • Encrypt data in transit and at rest for scoped systems.
  • Enforce least-privilege access with audit trails.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does PCI scope clarity matter?
checkpoint.answer: It determines where strict controls, auditability, and security obligations are mandatory.

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Fraud in Retail Payments
chapters.content:
Why Fraud Matters

Fraud directly impacts:

  • Revenue
  • Customer Trust
  • Operational Cost
  • Legal Exposure
  • Common Fraud Types

Stolen Card Usage

Criminal uses stolen card credentials.

Friendly Fraud

Customer claims:

"I Didn't Make This Purchase"

Despite making purchase.

Gift Card Fraud

Examples:

Balance Theft

  • Re-Encoded Cards
  • Refund Fraud

Examples:

Fake Returns

  • Receipt Manipulation
  • Employee Fraud

Examples:

Fake Refunds

  • Fake Void Transactions
  • Fraud Indicators
  • Unusual Transaction Velocity

Example:

  • 20 High-Value Purchases
  • In 5 Minutes
  • Excessive Refund Activity

Pattern:

  • Employee Processes
  • Large Numbers Of Refunds
  • High Decline Followed By Approval

Possible indicator:

Card Testing

Fraud Signal Families

  • Velocity anomalies (rapid repeated attempts)
  • Card-testing patterns (many declines then selective approvals)
  • Geographic/device inconsistencies
  • Refund abuse and return-linked payment anomalies

Detection + Action Design

  • Separate hard blocks from soft-review actions.
  • Persist reason codes for decision explainability.
  • Measure false-positive business cost alongside fraud prevention gain.

checkpoint.prompt: What is a common card-testing indicator?
checkpoint.answer: Large decline volumes followed by intermittent approvals.

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Severity Classification
chapters.content:
Payment incidents require prioritization.

Severity 1 (Critical)

Examples:

  • All Stores Cannot Process Payments
  • Major Gateway Outage
  • Nationwide Failure

Impact:

Immediate Revenue Loss

Response:

War Room

  • Executive Escalation

Severity 2 (High)

Examples:

Regional Outage

  • Major Tender Type Failure

Severity 3 (Medium)

Examples:

Store-Specific Issue

  • Intermittent Failures

Severity 4 (Low)

Examples:

  • Minor Configuration Issue
  • Single Terminal Issue

Objective Severity Inputs

  • Failed payment rate and transaction volume impact
  • Store/channel coverage of incident
  • Revenue-at-risk and compliance risk exposure
  • Customer harm potential (double charge, blocked checkout)

Escalation Rule

Severity assignment must be reproducible by different responders using the same incident facts.

checkpoint.answer: Revenue-at-risk multiplied by scope and customer impact.

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Retail Payment KPIs
chapters.content:
Authorization Rate

Approved Transactions
---------------------
Authorization Attempts
Settlement Success Rate
Settled Transactions
--------------------
Captured Transactions
Chargeback Rate

Measures disputed payments.

Lower is better.

Payment Latency

Measures response time.

High latency increases checkout friction.

Tender Mix

Tracks payment types:

  • Cash
  • Debit
  • Credit
  • Mobile Wallet
  • Gift Card

Used for business planning.

KPI Interpretation

  • Approval rate drop with steady traffic often signals gateway/issuer path degradation.
  • Timeout rate rise with stable decline rates suggests connectivity or latency regressions.
  • Chargeback spikes after promo periods may indicate fraud or authorization/capture handling gaps.

Minimum KPI Suite

  • Authorization approval rate
  • Timeout rate
  • Capture success rate
  • Settlement completion rate
  • Chargeback rate
  • Reconciliation variance aging

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Quick Quiz
chapters.content:
Quick Quiz

Choose one answer for each question. The correct answer is marked with (Correct).

Q1

Authorization means:

  • A. Funds settled
  • B. Payment is allowed/reserved (Correct)
  • C. Reconciliation completed
  • D. Chargeback closed

Q2

Capture is the step where:

  • A. Item is packed
  • B. Funds transfer is requested (Correct)
  • C. PAN is tokenized only
  • D. Receipt is voided

Q3

Missing settlement after successful sales creates:

  • A. Store layout issues
  • B. Cashflow and reconciliation risk (Correct)
  • C. Better conversion
  • D. Lower latency

Q4

PCI DSS primarily protects:

  • A. Shelf replenishment
  • B. Cardholder data (Correct)
  • C. Vendor SLAs
  • D. Promo stackability

Q5

A likely card-testing signal is:

  • A. Stable approvals
  • B. Decline spike followed by intermittent approvals (Correct)
  • C. High inventory turnover
  • D. More BOPIS pickups

checkpoint.prompt: What is the fastest way to explain payment failure impact?
checkpoint.answer: Translate decline/timeout metrics into affected stores, failed transactions, and revenue-at-risk.
